stem: A 60-year-old man who has smoked two packs a day for forty years has a cough and weight loss. Chest CT shows a central hilar mass with mediastinal nodes. Potassium is 2.9 mEq/L, blood pressure is raised and serum ACTH is high. Biopsy shows sheets of small blue cells with scant cytoplasm and nuclear molding.
oneliner: 60M + heavy smoker + central hilar mass + hypokalemia + high ACTH + small blue cells with nuclear molding → which immunostain?
ask: Which immunostain result is most likely on the biopsy?

whyNot.A: **CK5/6 and p40** mark squamous cell carcinoma, which forms keratin pearls; these cells are small and molded
whyNot.B: **CD45-positive** cells are lymphoid; a central tumor with ectopic ACTH is neuroendocrine
whyNot.C: **S-100 and HMB-45** are melanoma markers; nothing suggests melanoma
whyNot.D: **CD15 and CD30** mark Reed-Sternberg cells, which are large with prominent nucleoli, unlike these small molded cells

answer: Chromogranin A, synaptophysin and CD56 positive (small cell lung carcinoma)
why: A **central mass in a smoker** with **ectopic ACTH** and small blue cells is **small cell carcinoma**, derived from **neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells**. They stain for **chromogranin A, synaptophysin, neuron-specific enolase and CD56**.

idea.rule: Small cell carcinoma = neuroendocrine markers: chromogranin, synaptophysin, NSE, CD56.
also: Ectopic ACTH and ADH (SIADH) are classic

stem: A 76-year-old man with known heart failure has had two weeks of increasing breathlessness and needs to sit upright to breathe comfortably. A chest radiograph shows blunting of the right costophrenic angle with a curved upper border, and the fluid layers along the dependent chest wall when he lies on his side.
oneliner: 76M + heart failure + 2 weeks dyspnea, CXR: right costophrenic blunting with meniscus, layers on decubitus → which chest exam findings?
ask: Which chest examination pattern is most likely over the right base?

options.A: Hyperresonant, reduced fremitus, absent breath sounds, trachea midline
options.B: Dull, reduced fremitus, reduced breath sounds, trachea midline
options.C: Dull, increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, trachea midline
options.D: Hyperresonant on both sides, reduced fremitus, prolonged expiration, trachea midline
options.E: Dull, reduced fremitus, reduced breath sounds, trachea pulled to the right

whyNot.A: Hyperresonance suggests **air**, not fluid; the film shows **layering fluid**
whyNot.C: Increased fremitus and bronchial sounds mean **solid lung conducting sound**; here there is fluid **between** lung and chest wall
whyNot.D: This is **air trapping** in both lungs; his abnormality is **one-sided** and dull
whyNot.E: A pulled trachea means **volume loss** (collapse); layering fluid on a decubitus film is a **free effusion**, not a shrunken lung

answer: Dull percussion with reduced breath sounds and fremitus over the fluid
why: Fluid between the lung and chest wall **damps sound** and vibration, so percussion is **dull**, breath sounds and **tactile fremitus are reduced**. A moderate effusion leaves the trachea midline (a very large one pushes it away); a collapsed lung would pull it toward the side.

idea.rule: Pleural effusion: dull, quiet, decreased fremitus; consolidation: dull but loud (bronchial sounds, increased fremitus); pneumothorax: hyperresonant and quiet.
also: Pneumothorax: hyperresonant, absent breath sounds, decreased fremitus
Lobar collapse: dull, trachea pulled toward the lesion

stem: A 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has had a productive cough for years, bringing up a cupful of thick green sputum most mornings, with occasional blood streaking. She has finger clubbing and coarse crackles over both lower zones. A high-resolution CT scan of the chest is done.
oneliner: 14F + cystic fibrosis + years of thick purulent sputum, hemoptysis, clubbing, coarse crackles → which CT finding?
ask: Which CT finding is most likely?

options.A: Subpleural basal honeycombing with traction changes
options.B: Enlarged lymph nodes at both hila with perilymphatic nodules
options.C: Airways wider than the adjacent pulmonary artery, with thick walls that do not taper
options.D: Calcified plaques along the diaphragmatic pleura
options.E: Upper-lobe centrilobular lucencies with thin walls

whyNot.A: Honeycombing is **fibrotic scarring**, typical of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, not of **chronic suppurative airway disease**
whyNot.B: Hilar nodes with perilymphatic nodules point to **sarcoidosis**; she has years of purulent sputum, not a granulomatous picture
whyNot.D: Calcified pleural plaques mean **asbestos exposure**, with no such history here
whyNot.E: Upper-lobe centrilobular lucencies are **emphysema** from smoking; her years of **purulent sputum** point to diseased airways instead

why: Cystic fibrosis causes thick secretions, chronic infection and inflammation that **destroy airway wall elasticity**, leaving permanently dilated bronchi. On CT the bronchus is **wider than its adjacent artery** (signet ring), walls are thickened, and the airways **fail to taper** (tram-track).

idea.rule: Bronchiectasis on CT: bronchus-to-artery ratio above 1, thick walls, no tapering toward the periphery.
also: Prior severe infection such as tuberculosis or necrotizing pneumonia

stem: A 6-week-old girl has a sweat chloride of 74 mmol/L (normal below 30). She had been recalled to clinic at 3 weeks of age because one result on her routine heel-prick blood spot, taken on day 2 of life, was abnormal.
oneliner: 6-week-old girl + recalled at 3 weeks after newborn blood-spot screen + sweat chloride 74 mmol/L → which screening result?
ask: Which newborn screening result most likely led to the recall?

whyNot.A: Trypsinogen **leaks** from an injured pancreas, so the screen is **raised**, not low
whyNot.B: Raised phenylalanine screens for **phenylketonuria**, which does not give a high sweat chloride
whyNot.C: Raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone screens for **congenital adrenal hyperplasia**, with a normal sweat test
whyNot.E: Raised TSH screens for **congenital hypothyroidism**, unrelated to a **sweat chloride of 74**

why: The sweat chloride above 60 mmol/L confirms **cystic fibrosis**. Thick secretions block pancreatic ducts before birth, so pancreatic trypsinogen leaks into blood and the **immunoreactive trypsinogen** is raised on the dried blood spot; a positive screen is followed by a sweat test or CFTR genetics.

idea.rule: CF newborn screen = raised IRT on the blood spot, confirmed with sweat chloride of at least 60 mmol/L.
also: Blood spot also screens PKU, hypothyroidism, CAH and galactosemia
CFTR mutation panel follows a high IRT
Meconium ileus may be the first sign
Pancreatic insufficiency leads to fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
